sections.history: Varaha Narasimha, also called Kroda Narasimha (kroda is a Sanskrit word for the boar), is one of the nine Narasimha shrines of Ahobilam in the Nallamala hills. It lies about a kilometre beyond the Upper Ahobilam temple, on the bank of the Bhavanasini stream, along the path that climbs towards Jwala Narasimha — so for most pilgrims it is the first shrine on the walk into the gorge. Like its neighbours it belongs to the circle of worship maintained by the Ahobila Matha, and its stone shrine is generally associated with the Vijayanagara period, when Ahobilam received sustained royal support.
sections.architecture: The shrine is set into the rock beside the stream: a small enclosure with a low entrance leading to a cave-like sanctum. The image is distinctive, for the Lord here bears the face of a boar rather than a lion, and Bhudevi, the Earth goddess, is with him. Some accounts describe a Lakshmi Narasimha in the same cave, so two forms may be seen together.
sections.legends: The tradition of this shrine joins two stories. As Varaha, Vishnu took the form of a boar to rescue the Earth goddess from the demon Hiranyaksha, who had dragged her beneath the cosmic waters; Hiranyaksha was the brother of Hiranyakashipu, whom the Lord later destroyed as Narasimha. Here, the sthala purana tells, the Lord appears in a form that remembers both deliverances. In the astrological reading of the nine shrines, Varaha Narasimha is linked with Rahu.
sections.festivals: Narasimha Jayanti and the annual Brahmotsavam of Ahobilam are the principal occasions, when the stream of pilgrims along the Bhavanasini path swells. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: The walk from Upper Ahobilam follows the stream through a narrowing gorge, over boulders and steps; it is about a kilometre and manageable for most pilgrims in dry weather. The sound of water is constant. Many continue from here to Jwala Narasimha, so plan time and water for the longer climb if you mean to go on.

visit.timings: Worship is offered daily; the shrine is reached on foot and is best visited in daylight. Confirm current timings locally, especially in the monsoon, when the stream rises.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Reach Lower Ahobilam by road via Allagadda (Nandyal is the nearest major railhead) and go up to Upper Ahobilam by local transport. The shrine is about a kilometre further on foot, beside the Bhavanasini stream.
